why: Every project meets surprises: late suppliers, people who leave, requirements that grow. Project managers are hired to see them coming, decide early and keep the plan honest. Interviews for project roles almost always ask how you manage risks, issues and change requests, and expect a structured, concrete answer.
outcome: tell a risk from an issue, an assumption and a dependency in a RAID log; write risks as cause-risk-effect statements; score them with probability × impact and expected monetary value; choose a response with an owner and a trigger; run a risk review; escalate an issue with a decision deadline; take a change request through impact analysis and the change board; and plan the people side of a change with ADKAR and Kotter.

lessons.title: Risk, issue, assumption, dependency: the RAID log
text: A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, affects at least one project objective (scope, time, cost, quality, benefits). It has not happened yet, so it has a probability. Most risks are threats (negative), but the PMBOK Guide and PRINCE2 also count opportunities: uncertain events that would help the project, such as a supplier discount or a reusable component.

An issue is something that has already happened, or is certain, and needs action: the test server is down, the sponsor has rejected the design, the budget was cut by 10 %. An issue has no probability; it has a severity and a deadline for a decision. A risk that occurs becomes an issue, which is why the two are tracked side by side.

An assumption is something the plan treats as true without proof: “the client provides the test data by 1 March”, “two developers are available full time”. A dependency is a link to work outside the team’s control: another project’s release, a vendor delivery, a legal approval. Every assumption and dependency hides a risk (“what if it is not true?”), so good project managers review them as often as the risks.

Many teams keep the four in one RAID log (Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies; some teams use the A for Actions and the D for Decisions). It can be a spreadsheet, a Jira or Azure DevOps board, or a tab of the project plan. What matters is one place, one owner per line, a date, and a review rhythm.
points: Risk = may happen (probability); issue = has happened (severity, decision needed).
An assumption is accepted as true without proof; a dependency is work the team does not control.
A risk that occurs turns into an issue: link the two lines.
RAID log = Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies in one place, each line with an owner and a date.
Interviewers often start with “What is the difference between a risk and an issue?”: answer with probability and timing, then an example.

example.code:
RAID log, CRM migration project                         Owner     Review
R  Risk        The data export from the old CRM may fail     Sara      weekly
                on records with special characters
A  Assumption  Sales team available for testing in week 12   Karim     weekly
I  Issue       Test server down since Monday: testing blocked Nour      daily
D  Dependency  Single sign-on needs the IT security release  Paul      weekly
                planned for 15 May
example.note: Four kinds of line, one owner each, a review rhythm. If the assumption on week 12 turns out false, it becomes an issue.

lessons.title: Identifying risks and writing them well
text: Risk identification starts at the beginning of the project and never stops. Common techniques: a risk workshop with the team and key stakeholders, interviews with experts, checklists and lessons learned from past projects, a review of the assumptions and dependencies, the plan itself (critical path, single points of failure), and a prompt list such as PESTLE (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental) or the risk breakdown structure of the organisation.

In a workshop, ask everyone to write risks silently first, then group and remove duplicates: the loudest voice should not decide what gets written. A pre-mortem works well: “It is six months from now and the project has failed. Why?” People find it easier to explain a failure than to predict one.

Vague risks (“resources”, “budget”, “the supplier”) cannot be scored or managed. Write each risk as a cause-risk-effect statement: “Because of <cause, a fact today>, <uncertain event> may occur, which would lead to <effect on an objective>.” The cause is certain, the risk is uncertain, the effect is what you measure. This separates what you can act on (the cause and the event) from what you report (the effect).

For example, “Because our only DBA also supports production, she may be pulled away during the migration weekend, which would delay go-live by at least two weeks.” The response becomes obvious: train a second person or book an external DBA. Compare it with “Resource risk”, which leads nowhere.
points: Sources: workshops, expert interviews, checklists, lessons learned, assumptions and dependencies, the plan.
Prompt lists such as PESTLE help a team think beyond technical risks.
Cause-risk-effect: “Because of <cause>, <event> may occur, which would lead to <effect>.”
A pre-mortem (“the project failed: why?”) surfaces risks people hesitate to say.
Identification is continuous: new phase, new supplier, new scope = new risks.

example.code:
Vague:  "Supplier risk"

Cause-risk-effect:
  Because  the hardware supplier ships from one factory that had
           stoppages last year (cause, a fact),
  the      servers may arrive after the 1 June install date (risk, uncertain),
  which    would delay go-live by 3 weeks and cost 25,000 EUR in extra
           contractor time (effect on time and cost).
example.note: Once the cause and the effect are written, the team can score the risk and choose a response.

lessons.title: Scoring risks: probability × impact, the heat map and EMV
text: Qualitative scoring rates each risk on two scales, often 1 to 5: probability (1 = rare, 5 = almost certain) and impact (1 = negligible, 5 = severe). The organisation defines what each level means, for example impact 4 = “delay over one month or cost over 10 % of the budget”. The score is probability × impact, from 1 to 25.

The heat map (probability-impact matrix) places each risk on a grid: red at the top right, amber in the middle, green at the bottom left. With a 5 × 5 grid, a common rule is green 1-4, amber 5-12, red 15-25. The thresholds express the organisation’s risk appetite; ISO 31000:2018 (Risk management, Guidelines) leaves them to each organisation, and so do the PMBOK Guide and PRINCE2.

Quantitative analysis puts numbers on the most important risks. Expected monetary value (EMV) = probability × impact in money: a 30 % chance of a 40,000 EUR penalty has an EMV of 12,000 EUR. Threats have negative EMV and opportunities positive EMV in the PMBOK convention; many registers simply keep positive amounts and a Type column. The sum of the threats’ EMV is a sound basis for the contingency reserve.

Scores are estimates, not facts. Ask for the reasoning behind a 4, compare scores across risks to check consistency, and look at proximity (how soon the risk could happen): a score of 12 that could hit next week deserves more attention than a 15 that cannot occur before next year. Large projects also use Monte Carlo simulation on the schedule and cost model.
points: Score = probability × impact, typically on 1-5 scales (1 to 25).
Heat map: green, amber, red zones set by the organisation’s risk appetite.
EMV = probability × monetary impact; sum of threat EMVs → contingency reserve.
Contingency reserve covers identified risks; management reserve covers unknown ones.
Add proximity: how soon the risk could occur.

example.code:
Impact →        1      2      3      4      5
Probability 5   5      10     15     20     25
Probability 4   4      8      12     16     20
Probability 3   3      6      9      12     15
Probability 2   2      4      6      8      10
Probability 1   1      2      3      4      5

Green 1-4   Amber 5-12   Red 15-25
R3 Data migration errors: P 4 x I 4 = 16 -> red
EMV of a 30 % chance of a 40,000 EUR penalty = 0.3 x 40,000 = 12,000 EUR
example.note: A 5 × 5 heat map with typical zones. The thresholds are a choice of the organisation, written in its risk management plan.

lessons.title: Risk responses, owners and triggers
text: For threats, the classic responses are: avoid (change the plan so the risk cannot occur: drop an untested technology, move a date), mitigate or reduce (lower the probability or the impact: a prototype, extra testing, a second supplier), transfer (give the financial impact to a third party: insurance, a fixed-price contract, a warranty) and accept (do nothing now, either passively or actively with a contingency reserve and a fallback plan). The PMBOK Guide adds escalate, for a threat outside the project manager’s authority; PRINCE2 calls mitigation “reduce” and lists a fallback plan as its own response.

For opportunities, the mirror responses are: exploit (make sure it happens: assign the best people to finish early and earn a bonus), enhance (raise its probability or benefit), share (give part of it to a partner better placed to capture it, such as a joint venture) and accept (take it if it comes). Escalate exists for opportunities too.

Every risk needs one risk owner: a named person, not a team, who watches the risk and makes sure the response is carried out. The owner can delegate actions (the risk actionee in PRINCE2), but stays accountable. A response is a set of actions with dates and a cost; if the action costs more than the risk’s EMV, question it.

A trigger (warning sign) tells you the risk is about to happen or has started: a supplier misses an intermediate milestone, a key person hands in notice, defects per test day rise. Write the trigger next to the fallback plan so nobody needs a meeting to act. After the response, the residual risk is what remains; some responses create secondary risks (a second supplier brings integration risk), which go into the register too.
points: Threats: avoid, mitigate (reduce), transfer, accept; escalate when it is beyond the project’s authority.
Opportunities: exploit, enhance, share, accept (and escalate).
One named owner per risk; actions with dates and costs.
Trigger = warning sign that starts the fallback plan.
Record residual and secondary risks after the response.

example.code:
Risk R1  Servers may arrive after the 1 June install date (P 4, I 3, score 12)
Owner      Paul (procurement lead)
Response   Mitigate: order 4 weeks earlier, weekly call with the supplier
Fallback   Rent cloud servers for the first month (cost 6,000 EUR)
Trigger    Supplier misses the 15 April factory test milestone
Residual   P 2, I 3, score 6 (amber)
Secondary  Cloud set-up needs a security review (new risk R9)
example.note: Response, fallback and trigger are written in advance: when the trigger fires, the owner acts at once.

lessons.title: The risk register in practice and risk reviews
text: The risk register is the working tool: one line per risk with an ID, the cause-risk-effect description, category, date raised, probability, impact, score (or EMV), proximity, owner, response, actions and due dates, trigger, residual score and status (open, closed, occurred). Keep it in a shared place and keep the columns the team actually fills; a perfect template nobody updates is worse than a simple one used weekly.

Review it on a rhythm: a short risk review in the weekly project meeting for the top risks and new ones, a full review at each phase gate or every month. For each risk ask: is it still valid, has the score changed, are the actions done, has a trigger fired, can it be closed? Close risks whose window has passed; do not let the register grow into hundreds of stale lines.

Report the top risks to the steering committee, not the whole register: the five to ten highest scores, what changed since last time, and the decisions needed from them. A trend (score last month → this month) and the total EMV against the remaining contingency show whether the project’s risk exposure is going up or down.

In Excel, the score and the summary lines are simple formulas: score = probability × impact, total EMV with SUMPRODUCT, the number of open red risks with COUNTIFS, the name of the top risk with INDEX/MATCH/MAX. In agile teams, risks are often discussed in sprint planning and retrospectives, and mitigation work goes into the backlog like any other item.
points: Columns: ID, description, owner, probability, impact, score, response, actions, trigger, status.
Weekly review of the top risks; full review at each phase gate or monthly.
Close risks whose window has passed; keep the register short and alive.
Steering committee: top risks, trend, decisions needed, EMV vs remaining contingency.
Agile teams put mitigation work in the backlog.

example.code:
E2  =C2*D2                                   score = probability x impact
H2  =INDEX(B2:B6,MATCH(MAX(E2:E6),E2:E6,0))  name of the top risk
H3  =COUNTIFS(E2:E6,">=15",F2:F6,"Open")    open risks in the red zone
H4  =SUMPRODUCT(J2:J6,K2:K6)                 total EMV (probability x cost)
example.note: B = risk name, C = probability, D = impact, E = score, F = status, J = probability in %, K = cost impact. Four formulas give the summary for the steering committee.

lessons.title: Issues and escalation
text: An issue log records each issue with an ID, description, date raised, raised by, type, severity or priority, owner, the decision or action needed, the date it is needed by, and status. PRINCE2 distinguishes three types of issue: requests for change, off-specifications (something the project will not deliver as specified) and problems or concerns. Many teams simply use severity levels such as critical, high, medium, low.

Handle an issue in steps: capture it, assess its impact on time, cost, scope, quality and benefits, decide (inside your authority) or escalate, then act and close. Speed matters more than polish: an issue is already costing time. Give every issue a decision deadline (“we need a decision by Thursday, otherwise the test phase slips one week”) so it does not sit in the log.

Escalation means taking a decision to the level that has the authority for it, not handing over blame. The escalation path is agreed at the start of the project: team lead → project manager → steering committee or sponsor. PRINCE2 uses tolerances (allowed deviation on time, cost, scope and other objectives): while a forecast stays within tolerance the project manager decides; when it is forecast to go beyond, the project manager raises an exception to the project board.

A good escalation is short and makes the decision easy: the facts, the impact, two or three options with their cost and consequences, your recommendation, and the deadline. Escalate early: senior people forgive bad news, they do not forgive surprises. After the decision, record it in the decision log and inform everyone affected.
points: Issue log: severity, owner, action or decision needed, decision deadline, status.
Steps: capture → assess impact → decide or escalate → act → close.
Escalate to the level with the authority, along a path agreed at the start.
PRINCE2: beyond tolerance → exception raised to the project board.
Escalation message: facts, impact, options, recommendation, deadline.

example.code:
To: Steering committee        Subject: Decision needed by Thu 14 March

Issue   The payment provider moved its API change to 2 April;
        our go-live is 25 March.
Impact  Go-live cannot pass the payment tests: 1 week delay at least.
Options A. Delay go-live to 8 April (no extra cost, marketing campaign moves)
        B. Go live on 25 March without card payments (bank transfer only)
        C. Pay the provider's early-access fee (8,000 EUR) to test now
Advice  Option C: inside the contingency, keeps the campaign date.
We need your decision by Thursday 14 March to keep option C open.
example.note: Facts, impact, options, recommendation and a deadline: the committee can decide in five minutes.

lessons.title: Change control: change requests and the change board
text: Once the scope, schedule and cost baselines are approved, any change to them goes through change control. A change request records what is asked, by whom, and why. Change requests come from customers, sponsors, regulation, defects or the team itself, and include corrective actions that change the baseline.

The project manager (or a business analyst) runs an impact analysis: effect on scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, risks and benefits, plus the options. For example, “add a mobile app” might mean 6 weeks and 45,000 EUR more, or the same date if two reports are dropped. Without this analysis, nobody can make a fair decision.

The decision is taken by the body with the authority: a change control board (CCB) in the PMBOK Guide’s terms, a change authority delegated by the project board in PRINCE2, often the steering committee or the sponsor for large changes. Small changes can be delegated to the project manager within agreed limits. The outcome is approved, rejected or deferred; if approved, update the baselines, the plan, the register and the contract if needed, then communicate.

Scope creep is scope that grows without going through this process: “a small extra field”, “just one more report”. Each looks harmless, together they eat the contingency. Gold plating is the team adding extras nobody asked for. The cure is the same: every change, even small, is logged and assessed. In agile delivery, change is expected: the product owner reorders the backlog, but within a fixed sprint and with the trade-off visible (something else moves out).
points: Change request → impact analysis → decision (CCB / change authority) → update baselines → implement → communicate.
Impact analysis covers scope, time, cost, quality, resources, risks and benefits, with options.
Decisions: approved, rejected or deferred, recorded in the change log.
Scope creep = uncontrolled growth of scope; gold plating = extras the team adds unasked.
Agile: change goes through the backlog, with the trade-off made visible.

example.code:
Change request CR-014                     Raised by: Sales director, 3 April
Request    Add export to Excel on the customer dashboard
Reason     Sales managers rebuild the figures by hand every week
Impact     Scope: +1 feature   Time: +8 days   Cost: +6,400 EUR
           Risk: touches the reporting module before the audit
Options    1. Add to release 2 (no impact on the current date)
           2. Add now and drop the PDF export (same date, same cost)
Decision   CCB 10 April: option 1 approved, baseline unchanged
example.note: The impact analysis turns a quick request into a decision with a visible price.

lessons.title: Organisational change management: the people side
text: A project can deliver on time and still fail if people do not use what it delivers. Organisational change management (conduite du changement in French companies) prepares, supports and equips the people whose work changes: users, their managers, support teams. It starts at the beginning of the project, not a week before go-live.

Prosci’s ADKAR model, created by Jeff Hiatt, follows each person through five outcomes: Awareness of the need for change, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to do it in daily work, and Reinforcement so the change sticks. It helps find where someone is blocked: a user who knows the new tool but has no time to practise lacks Ability, not Knowledge.

John Kotter’s eight steps (Leading Change, 1996) look at the organisation: create a sense of urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a vision and strategy, communicate the vision, empower people by removing obstacles, generate short-term wins, consolidate gains and keep going, and anchor the new ways in the culture. In practice, project teams use the ideas in general terms: a visible sponsor, a clear reason, early wins, and leaders who act the change.

The tools are a stakeholder and impact analysis (who is affected, how much, what they lose), a communication plan (message, audience, channel, sender, date), training at the right time, change champions in each team, and feedback channels. Resistance is normal: listen to understand it (fear of losing skills, workload, past failed projects), answer the real concern and involve people in the solution. Measure adoption after go-live: logins, use of the new process, support tickets.
points: Success = people adopt the change, not just “delivered on time”.
ADKAR (Prosci): Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
Kotter’s 8 steps: urgency, coalition, vision, communication, remove obstacles, short-term wins, keep going, anchor in culture.
Tools: impact analysis, communication plan, training, champions, feedback.
Resistance is information: find the cause and involve people.

example.code:
Change: new expense tool for 600 employees, go-live 1 September

ADKAR stage    Action                                      When
Awareness      CFO video: why the old process is costly   June
Desire         Managers explain what changes for the team  July
               (faster refunds, no paper)
Knowledge      20-minute e-learning + quick guide          August
Ability        Champions' drop-in hours, first claims      September
               checked together
Reinforcement  Refund-time dashboard, old forms removed    October

Adoption KPI: 90 % of claims in the new tool by 31 October
example.note: One action per ADKAR stage, timed with the project plan, and a measure of adoption at the end.

pitfalls: Writing vague risks (“resources”, “budget”) that cannot be scored, owned or acted on.
Logging issues in the risk register (or risks in the issue log): something that has already happened has no probability.
Giving a risk to “the team” or “IT”: without one named owner, nobody acts.
Filling the register at kick-off and never reviewing it again, or letting it fill with hundreds of stale lines.
Accepting “small” changes without a change request: scope creep eats the contingency one request at a time.
Escalating late, or escalating a problem without options and a decision deadline.
Treating change management as a training session the week before go-live.

exercises.q: In E2, the risk score of R1 (probability × impact).
exercises.hint: Score = probability × impact. Use the cells, not the typed numbers.
exercises.explain: 4 × 3 = 12, in the amber zone of a 5 × 5 heat map (5-12). Copied down, the formula gives 10 for R2 and 12 for R3.

exercises.q: In G2, the name of the risk with the highest score.
exercises.hint: MAX finds the highest score, MATCH(…, 0) finds its row, INDEX returns the name from that row.
exercises.explain: The highest score is 16, in the third row of the range, so the result is “Data migration errors”. XLOOKUP(MAX(E2:E6),E2:E6,B2:B6) gives the same. With a tie, both return the first risk found: show the top five, not only one.

exercises.q: In E2, the total expected monetary value (EMV) of these four threats: probability × cost impact, added up.
exercises.hint: SUMPRODUCT multiplies the two ranges row by row and adds the results.
exercises.explain: 12000 + 12000 + 4000 + 5000 = 33000 EUR. Note that two very different risks (30 % × 40000 and 10 % × 120000) have the same EMV: EMV ranks average cost, so still look at the worst case of high-impact risks.

exercises.q: In G2, the number of risks that are both still open and in the red zone (score 15 or more).
exercises.hint: COUNTIFS(range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2): the score at least 15 and the status Open.
exercises.explain: R1 (16), R4 (20) and R7 (15) are open with a score of 15 or more: 3. R2 and R6 are red but closed. Write ">=15", not ">15", or R7 is missed.

exercises.q: In G2, the contingency reserve the PMO asks for: the EMV of the threats minus the EMV of the opportunities.
exercises.hint: Two SUMIFS on the EMV column: one for the Threat rows, one for the Opportunity rows.
exercises.explain: Threats 12000 + 9000 + 6000 = 27000, opportunities 4000, contingency 23000 EUR. This follows the PMBOK sign convention (threats negative, opportunities positive). Some organisations do not count opportunities and keep the full 27000: the rule belongs in the risk management plan.

exercises.q: A risk has a 25 % probability and a cost impact of 80,000 EUR. What is its expected monetary value, in EUR?
exercises.answer: EMV = 0.25 × 80,000 = 20,000 EUR. It is an average over many risks, not the amount you will lose: this one will cost either 0 or 80,000.

exercises.q: Match each risk response with an example.
pairs: Replace an untested beta library with the supported version, so the risk cannot occur
Run a load test in month 2 and add a second server to lower the chance of a slowdown
Sign a fixed-price contract so the supplier bears any cost overrun
Keep 5,000 EUR of contingency and monitor; no action now
Put the best team on the critical path to be sure to earn the early-delivery bonus
Bid with a partner firm to win a larger contract neither could win alone
exercises.answer: Avoid removes the cause, mitigate lowers probability or impact, transfer moves the financial impact, accept keeps the risk (with a reserve when active). For opportunities, exploit makes it certain and share involves a partner better placed to capture it.

exercises.q: Sort these lines between the risk register and the issue log.

groups.name: Risk
items: The vendor may raise its licence prices at renewal
Users may not have time for training during the busy season
The new regulation might require extra audit logs

groups.name: Issue
items: The test server has been down since Monday
The sponsor rejected the design at yesterday’s review
Two developers resigned and leave on Friday

exercises.answer: Risks are uncertain (may, might, could) and have a probability. Issues have happened or are certain, and need an action or a decision now. When a risk occurs, close it in the register and open an issue that refers to it.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a change request in order.
steps: Log the change request with its reason and requester
Analyse the impact on scope, time, cost, quality and risks
Present options to the change board, which approves, rejects or defers
Update the baselines, the plan and the registers
Implement the change and communicate it to the stakeholders
Check the result and close the change request
exercises.answer: Nothing is built before the decision, and the baselines are updated before the work starts, so progress is measured against the approved plan.

exercises.q: Three weeks before the planned installation, the hardware supplier tells you the servers may arrive two weeks late.

choices.label: Get the facts: how likely, how late, why, and what the supplier can do; check the register for this risk and its fallback
choices.feedback: This was a known risk (R1): its response and trigger should already be written. Facts first, then impact.

choices.label: Tell the steering committee the project will be two weeks late
choices.feedback: Too early: you do not yet know the probability, the impact on the critical path or the options.

choices.label: Wait: the supplier only said “may”
choices.feedback: A warning from the supplier is exactly the kind of trigger the register should name. Waiting removes options.

steps.text: The delay is likely and the installation is on the critical path. Go-live would slip two weeks. What next?

choices.label: Assess the options: start the fallback plan (rented cloud servers, 6,000 EUR), re-sequence other tasks, or ask the supplier to ship part of the order early
choices.feedback: Options with cost and effect on the date let someone decide quickly.

choices.label: Ask the team to work weekends to catch up after delivery
choices.feedback: Overtime on a late, unknown date is a hidden cost and a quality risk; it is not a plan.

steps.text: The fallback costs 6,000 EUR; your authority goes up to 5,000 EUR. What do you do?

choices.label: Escalate to the sponsor with the facts, the options, your recommendation and a decision deadline, and update the risk and issue logs
choices.feedback: Beyond your authority: escalate early, with a clear recommendation, and record the decision.

choices.label: Split the cost into two orders of 3,000 EUR to stay within your limit
choices.feedback: That bypasses the governance you agreed to; it destroys trust when discovered.

exercises.answer: Treat the warning as the trigger of a known risk: get the facts, assess the impact on the critical path, compare options, then decide within your authority or escalate with a recommendation and a deadline. Record it: the risk becomes an issue, and the decision goes into the decision log.

exercises.q: In ADKAR, a user has attended the training and understands the new tool, but keeps using the old spreadsheet because there is no time to practise. Which element is missing?
exercises.answer: Knowledge is there (training done, understood); Ability, being able to do it in daily work, is missing. Give practice time, support from a champion, and check the first real uses together.

exercises.q: Your project moves a warehouse to a new stock management system. Write three risks as cause-risk-effect statements, each with a score (probability and impact, 1-5), a response type, an owner and a trigger.
exercises.answer:
1) Because the old system holds 15 years of item codes with duplicates, the data migration may load wrong stock levels, which would cause wrong picking and missed deliveries in the first weeks. P 4, I 4 = 16. Mitigate: cleansing sprint and two trial migrations with reconciliation reports. Owner: data lead. Trigger: more than 1 % mismatch in trial migration 1.
2) Because go-live falls in November, the busiest month, staff may not have time to learn the scanners, which would slow picking and raise errors. P 3, I 4 = 12. Avoid: move go-live to January (approved change). Owner: operations manager. Trigger: the date is confirmed by the business.
3) Because the scanners come from one supplier with a 10-week lead time, they may arrive after the install date, which would delay go-live by at least three weeks. P 2, I 4 = 8. Transfer the cost (late-delivery penalty in the contract) and mitigate (order now). Owner: procurement lead. Trigger: no shipping confirmation four weeks before the install.
A strong answer has a cause that is a fact, an uncertain event, a measurable effect, and responses that match the score.

interview.q: What is the difference between a risk and an issue?
interview.a: A risk is uncertain and in the future: it has a probability and an impact, and I manage it with a response planned in advance. An issue has already happened or is certain: it has a severity and needs action or a decision now. For example, “the lead developer may leave” is a risk; “the lead developer resigned today” is an issue. When a risk occurs I close it in the register, open an issue that refers to it, and start the fallback plan written for it.

interview.q: How do you identify risks on a new project?
interview.a: At kick-off I run a workshop with the team and key stakeholders, often as a pre-mortem, and I add lessons learned from similar projects, a checklist or PESTLE prompt list, and a review of the plan’s assumptions, dependencies and critical path. I write each risk as cause-risk-effect so it can be scored and owned. Then identification continues: every weekly meeting asks “anything new?”, and each new phase, supplier or scope change gets its own review.

I score probability and impact on the organisation’s scales and place risks on the heat map, then I look at proximity: a risk that could occur next week comes before one that cannot occur for months. For the top risks with a cost impact I calculate the expected monetary value, and I use the total to check that the contingency reserve is enough. I challenge the scores in the review, because they are estimates, and I keep a close eye on low-probability, very high-impact risks that EMV tends to understate.

interview.q: Tell me about a time a risk turned into an issue.
interview.a: Use STAR. For example: our data migration depended on a vendor export tool (situation). We had logged the risk that it would fail on large tables, with a trial migration as mitigation and a fallback of a manual SQL extract (task). In the trial it failed on two tables: the trigger fired, I opened an issue, started the fallback and briefed the sponsor the same day with the impact (two extra days) and the cost (inside the contingency) (action). We kept the go-live date, and the lesson learned went into the PMO checklist (result).

interview.q: How do you handle a change request from an important stakeholder?
interview.a: I thank them, log it, and make sure I understand the need behind the request. Then I run an impact analysis on scope, time, cost, quality and risks, with options, for example later release, or now in exchange for something else. The decision goes to the body with the authority, the change board or the sponsor, not to me alone and not to the requester alone. If approved, I update the baselines and communicate. The stakeholder gets a fair decision with a visible price, and the project avoids scope creep.

interview.q: When do you escalate, and how?
interview.a: When a decision is beyond my authority or a forecast goes beyond the agreed tolerance on time, cost or scope, and as early as possible. I follow the escalation path agreed at the start. My message is short: the facts, the impact, two or three options with their cost and consequences, my recommendation and the date by which we need a decision. Then I record the decision and tell everyone affected. Senior people accept bad news; they do not accept surprises.

interview.q: How do you make sure people actually adopt what the project delivers?
interview.a: I plan change management from the start with the business sponsor: an impact analysis of who is affected and how, a communication plan, training close to go-live, and change champions in each team. I use ADKAR to see where people are blocked, for example they know the tool but lack the time to practise, which is Ability, not Knowledge. I treat resistance as information and look for the real concern. After go-live I measure adoption, such as usage and support tickets, and keep reinforcing until the old way is gone.
